newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Central Eastern European bourses bearish.
newsitem.headline: Central Eastern European bourses bearish.

text.p: Bourses in Central and Eastern Europe fell sharply this week despite positive corporate earnings reports and stock market gains elsewhere in Europe after the U.S. left its short-term interest rates unchanged.
The Central European Share (CESI) index which reflects the price movements of 73 Czech, Polish, Hungarian, Slovak and Slovenian stocks, fell 3.55 percent.
BUDAPEST
Hungarian share prices were slack this week as two days of falls were followed by two days of rises. The BUX index declined 25.28 points to finish at 3,581 points on Thursday.
The January-September corporate results failed to boost the market and traders said the market had run out of steam.
"I don't think we can expect significant rises or falls in the near term," said Peter Lencs of MKB Securities.
WARSAW
Polish shares fell 3.5 percent this week and analysts said they could stabilise or fall next week as investors were likely to wait for 1997 tax bills to come into law.
They said Thursday's vote in the Senate on 1997 taxes, amending a previous lower-house bill seen as inflationary, could bring some optimism to the market.
Analysts expected October's monthly earnings reports, due Monday, to prove good, which could spur a brief rebound.
PRAGUE
Czech shares slid sharply throughout the week with the closely watched PX50 index falling nearly four percent.
Dealers and analysts were virtually unanimous in attributing the decline to structural problems on the Czech capital markets rather than to company fundamentals.
BRATISLAVA

The Slovak Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) saw another week of dull trading with insignificant activity of foreign players, and brokers predicted no reversal of the bourse's long-term downward trend over the next few weeks.
The 12-share index fell 0.86 points to 188.98 on Thursday, from the Monday's open at 189.84, after slight increases to above the 190 point level on Monday and Tuesday.
Dealers cited low activity of foreign investors - echoeing bearish sentiment in neighbouring markets, changes to securities legislation and expectations of further price declines.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks closed mostly lower on Thursday after mixed trading through the week, but blue chips Zagrebacka Banka and drug firm Pliva resisted the downward trend.
The traders predicted most stocks would recover as the government, in a drive against fraud, attempted to dispel fears saying no bona fide share purchases would be challenged.
Share prices plumetted two weeks ago when privatisation officials said they would annul some 9,000 employee buyout contracts, driving away foreign buyers.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares fell 4.11 percent after the unofficial results of Sunday's general election showed the ruling Liberal Democrats may have to relinquish power to the right-wing "Spring" alliance.
"If right-wing parties take over, shares may fall due to uncertainty about the future government policy," a trader said.
The SBI index closed at 1,173.7 on Thursday, down 50.18.
BUCHAREST
Light investor interest kept turnover thin at 54.6 million lei ($15,730) on Tuesday and sent it even lower to 31.2 million on Thursday, when low demand met with even lower supply.
Azomures SA took the bulk of trade on both days.
Seven stocks inched up, sending unofficial indices VAB and BIG on Thursday each up 0.7 percent from the previous session.
SOFIA

Floor trading was suspended on October 23 by the trading regulatory body after public share companies failed to meet new legal requirements by the September 19 deadline. Since then only sporadic repo deals in government securities were struck.
